A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same design-based inference framework despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte Carlo coverage and variance-reduction results in Section 5 and Table 2, plus an analysis of production OOM telemetry in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports simulation coverage across 200 treatment-assignment resamples in Section 5 and retains the OOM telemetry analysis in Section 6.

M1.justification: The IPW/AIPW formulas and normal-mixture union-bound construction remain unchanged; identifying AIPW as generally oracle changes its applicability claim rather than its algorithm. Corollary 4.10 makes a limited inference-output correction by explicitly returning p = 1 when the inversion set is empty.

E1.justification: Dataset 5.1 now includes units whose events never occur, with probabilities 0.20 under control and 0.35 under treatment. This revises the simulated population beyond delayed finite events. The delayed-reward task and OOM telemetry dataset remain; moving the latter into Section 6 adds no dataset.

E2.justification: The empirical IPW-versus-event-time-AIPW comparison in v1 Table 2 is removed, leaving IPW alone in the main simulation. Classical pointwise intervals, the variance-upper-bound benchmark, and the Lindon and Kallus (2025) Poisson comparison remain.

E3.justification: Section 5 narrows the reported evaluation from IPW and running-mean AIPW, each with oracle and estimated variance coverage, to one IPW coverage assessment. The retained design still resamples assignments with fixed potential outcomes, using 500 units, Uniform(0,10) entry times, balanced randomization, and the same nominal coverage levels.

E4.justification: The central augmentation analysis testing whether running-mean adjustment reduces interval width while preserving coverage is withdrawn, along with the explicit oracle-versus-estimated variance coverage comparison. The reward–time dependence analysis, resampled trajectories, martingale-violation example, and OOM case study remain despite relocation and redrawing.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly states 200 assignment resamples for its coverage estimates; v1 does not specify the replication count underlying Table 2. This is newly reported run information, not an established increase: the 100 paths in v1 Figure 2 are retained as 100 paths in v2 Figure 4. Neither version reports Monte Carlo confidence intervals for coverage rates.

E6.justification: v1 Table 2 reports estimated-variance IPW coverage of 96.8%, 97.9%, and 99.7% for control, treatment, and their difference; v2 Section 5 reports 96.0%, 97.0%, and 99.0%. These replace results under a changed synthetic population, so they do not establish same-setting deterioration. AIPW coverage results and the reported 86%, 76%, and 83% width reductions are removed. Synthetic plots change, while the OOM findings remain.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.4 changes from a cumulative-process equivalence to a unit-level characterization with explicit predictability and conditional-propensity assumptions, with a revised Appendix A.1 proof. Lemma 4.5 changes its boundedness condition to residual jumps and strengthens the stated approximation remainder. Proposition 4.12 and Appendix A.5 generalize two special variance regimes to arbitrary limiting variance shares, proving a limiting relative width at most one.

C1.justification: v1 presents covariate-adjusted variance reduction as a practical contribution in its abstract, introduction, and conclusion. v2 limits the directly observable method covered by its theory to IPW, retains AIPW as an oracle characterization, and defers practical variance reduction to future work. Its conclusion also strengthens the asymptotic width comparison beyond the earlier special cases.

C2.justification: v2 explains that nontrivial event-time augmentation generally requires unobserved counterfactual event times and that entry-frozen augmentation introduces error outside the current argument. Section 4.3 explicitly identifies the variance-upper-bound curve as a benchmark rather than a valid confidence-sequence boundary. Section 4.2 also acknowledges degenerate exceptions to the nonmartingale obstruction.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the new never-event probabilities but omits v1's simulation mixture tuning value eta-squared = 1/16 and shock widths 0.5 and 0.3. These omissions reduce reproducibility detail; they do not establish that the omitted parameter values changed. No code or data access resource is added.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to design-based inference, survival analysis, and counting-process methods are retained. The logrank reference changes from its 2020 preprint to the 2024 publication of the same work; other reference changes are bibliographic corrections or formatting.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, Section 4 substantially expands and reorganizes the filtration explanation, the simulation description becomes a structured list, and the conclusion is extensively rewritten. The OOM case study moves from Appendix C into its own main-text section, while its Poisson comparison remains in the appendix.

P2.justification: The two-column main text becomes single-column, with extensive reflow and resized displays. Table 2 is removed, synthetic figures are redrawn with changed axes and trajectories, and several displays move between the main text and appendices. The reward-dependence and OOM figures move into the main text, while the sample-path boundary comparison moves to Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important practical overclaim: v1 promotes and quantifies usable AIPW variance reduction, whereas v2 explains its dependence on unavailable counterfactual event times and limits practical guarantees to IPW. It also clarifies the benchmark's inferential status and supplies a more general relative-width theorem and proof. Although some simulation specifications are lost, the clearer separation of implementable inference from oracle results substantially improves the paper's scientific reliability.
